title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
Here's my conversation with @latkins and the team at @arcee_ai on their path to training and releasing Trinity Large today.
From going all in on open models built end to end in the US 6 months ago to having the model in hand is no easy feet.
I loved this conversation on how to design a startup around open models and take a bold step to scale it up. I'm openly an Arcee fan, watching them take risk and pull it off.
We discuss:
- The state (and future) of open vs. closed models,
- The business of selling open models for on-prem deployments,
- The story of Arcee AI & going “all-in” on this training run,
- The ATOM project,
- Building frontier model training teams in 6 months,
- and other great topics. I really loved this one, and think you well too.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
ARCEE TRINITY LARGE
Model (Open weights)
- ~400B total parameters
- ~13B active per token
- Decoder-only MoE
- Trained end-to-end (not distilled)
Checkpoints:
- TrueBase: 10T tokens, pre-anneal, no instruction or RL, no long-context support
- Base: 17T tokens, full pretrained foundation model
- Preview: lightly post-trained, chat-ready, under active RL
Attention stack
- GQA
- QK-Norm
- Gated attention (Qwen G1)
- 3:1 local/global pattern
- Local: RoPE + sliding window
- Global: NoPE
- Window: 4096
Well-engineered integration of standard attention mechanisms.
MoE
- 256 experts, 4 active (4-of-256, 1.56% routing sparsity)
- 1 always-on shared expert
- Sigmoid routing
Experts are larger and coarser in Trinity Large (fewer activated) to maximize throughput.
This is why it’s technically sparse, not computationally sparse. 13B active per token means dense-13B compute every step, with a large expert bank behind it.
Main novelty: SMEBU (Soft-clamped Momentum Expert Bias Updates)
Replaces sign-based bias updates with smooth, momentum-stabilized, normalized updates.
Purpose: stabilize routing, prevent oscillation and expert collapse, and enable stable large-scale MoE training.
Stability engineering
- Muon as the primary optimizer
- AdamW only for embeddings and output
- QK-Norm to control Muon-amplified attention logit instability
- z-loss added mid-training to cap logit growth
- Dense layers increased 3 → 6 for stability
Data: 17T tokens from a 20T curated mix, heavily synthetic: 6.5T web, 1T multilingual, 800B code. Strong math/code/STEM bias with broad multilingual coverage.
RSDB (Random Sequential Document Buffer) is a system-level training contribution that fixes batch imbalance, gradient instability, long-document bias, and loss spikes. It reduces batch imbalance by 4.23× and step variance by 2.4×, directly improving training smoothness and stability.
Context is pretrained at 8K and extended to 256K (trained), 512K (generalizes), and 1M (partial). MK-NIAH: 0.994 at 256K, 0.976 at 512K, 0.42 at 1M, shows generalization far beyond the training context.
Training runs on 2048× B300 GPUs with FSDP and expert parallelism. Inference uses FP8 and a vLLM backend, with benchmarks on 8× H200.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
Anthropic just released the receipts on a fear everyone’s been hand-waving.
52 junior engineers learning a new Python library. AI group scored 50% on comprehension tests. Manual coding group scored 67%. That’s a 17% gap on foundational skills, and debugging showed the steepest decline.
The productivity trade looked even worse. The AI group finished only two minutes faster on average, and that difference didn’t reach statistical significance. Several developers spent up to 30% of their time just composing queries.
Here’s what actually matters: they identified three failure patterns that predicted sub-40% scores. Fully delegating code to AI. Starting independently but progressively offloading work. Using AI as a debugging crutch without building understanding. All three share a common thread: removing the cognitive struggle that produces learning.
The high scorers (65%+) did something different. Some generated code first, then asked follow-up questions to understand what they’d produced. Others requested explanations alongside the code. The fastest group asked only conceptual questions, then coded independently while troubleshooting their own errors.
The gap between “AI makes you faster” and “AI helps you learn” turns out to be enormous. And most workflows are optimized entirely for the former.
Quoting @AnthropicAI
AI can make work faster, but a fear is that relying on it may make it harder to learn new skills on the job.
We ran an experiment with software engineers to learn more. Coding with AI led to a decrease in mastery—but this depended on how people used it.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
NVIDIA just told you Blackwell is mandatory for efficient inference and nobody’s repricing.
The paper shows 99.4% accuracy going from 16-bit to 4-bit. That’s the headline. Here’s what matters: NVFP4 is a Blackwell-native format. The Tensor Cores on Blackwell GPUs handle FP4 operations directly with zero dequantization overhead. Every other GPU has to upconvert those 4-bit weights to 16-bit before computing.
The math:
∙ 3.5x memory reduction vs FP16
∙ 1.8x reduction vs FP8
∙ 2.3x faster inference throughput
But only on Blackwell.
Run NVFP4 on an H100? You lose the throughput advantage. The weights decompress, the memory bandwidth chokes, and you’re back to FP8 economics.
This tells you everything about NVIDIA’s inference strategy. They’re not just selling compression research. They’re building format lock-in into the silicon. Every model checkpoint published in NVFP4 becomes a Blackwell advertisement.
The paper authors include Bryan Catanzaro and Song Han. This came from NVIDIA Research with production intent baked in. Hugging Face already hosts NVFP4 checkpoints for DeepSeek-R1, Llama 3, and FLUX.
Cloud providers have two choices: upgrade to Blackwell and serve at half the memory cost, or run legacy hardware at 2x the footprint. The ROI math forces the upgrade.
Anyone reading this as “cool compression paper” is missing the game. NVIDIA just made their latest silicon the only efficient way to run quantized inference at scale.
Quoting @elliotarledge
NVIDIA just dropped a banger paper on how they compressed a model from 16-bit to 4-bit and were able to maintain 99.4% accuracy, which is basically lossless.
This is a must read. Link below.

> Some companies hire heavily out of Twitter, some hire from communities such as GPU Mode or NanoGPT speedrunning.
To Nathan's point, I am leading an open source workgroup within the @GPU_MODE community (#teenygrad channel) in order to develop a deep learning systems course with an MIT-licensed book, codebase, and lectures which develops your own deep learning framework teenygrad from scratch which can run nanogpt. The project has access to some compute thanks to to the @LambdaAPI research grant (thank you @chuanli11)
This project has been a labor of love the past few months, bridging a must-needed pedagogical gap from micrograd to tinygrad. The SITP book develops teenygrad framework step by step, from a numpy clone, to a pytorch1 clone, to a pytorch2 style compiler. The SITP philosophy subscribes to the same views as @karpathy on education: it's a technical problem whose solution requires a ramp with empathy:
> ..education is the very difficult technical process of building ramps to knowledge...I feel like education is..a tangle of understanding and you're trying to lay it out in a way that creates a ramp where everything only depends on the thing before it.
The project's primary challenge for better and for worse has been the breadth of scope. A lot of time was spent "curriculum engineering", and we are now just getting to implementing accelerated cpu and gpu kernels with automatic differentiation in earnest, but it has a good line of sight towards fusion compilation using tinygrad's RISCy IR. The good news for you is that now is a perfect time to help the workgroup, and to come join in learning from the best. There are some heavy hitters here led by @marksaroufim, @m_sirovatka, @a1zhang, @gaunernst and more.

summary:
A different way to think about agi:
What if agi was not a model but a process. The process of learning and recursively improves autonomously. What if instead of being a model that can one shoot any task agi is rather an algorithm that can learn to solve anything
I think variants of our current algorithm are powerful enough to learn any task, given sufficient compute and time for models to interact with the real world.
So I would argue agi is already here. Yes there is still a human in the loop, but recursive self improvement has already started. Older generation models were already used to filter new generation pretraining data, current agentic models are used to build semi autonomously new long horizon RL tasks. The autonomous fly wheel to super intelligence has already started years ago and we are gradually removing the training wheels.
It's also misleading to hope that by a given date we will have a model that can one shot any task, there is a long tail of problems that will take time to learn even with many more orders of magnitude of compute, the learning signal from the physical world is slower and simulation is only an imperfect approximations. You don't "solve" math there will always be new problems that will require one oom more intelligence to be solved. You don't one shot science, some scientific discovery will cost hundreds of billions in compute to be solved and we will have to prioritize which one we solve first
Quoting @polynoamial
Francois Chollet: "AGI ~2030"
Folks often point to @fchollet as an AGI skeptic, but he's said multiple times that he thinks it arrives within 5 years.
The AI we have today is not AGI, but it's progressing very quickly.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
I was two days too early to conclude that the frontier LLM architectures have largely converged.
So I dug through @Alibaba_Qwen Qwen 3.5 (397B-A17B)'s source code too.
Here's a detailed breakdown of what makes it different, and what it shares with other frontier models.
TL;DR: This is architecturally the most distinctive frontier MoE model of 2025/2026 — while GLM-5 largely follows DeepSeek-V3, Qwen went in a genuinely different direction.
---
1. HYBRID ATTENTION: THE DEFINING BET
Qwen 3.5's most radical choice is replacing 75% of attention layers with Gated DeltaNet linear attention.
The model has 60 layers with a [Linear, Linear, Linear, Full] × 15 pattern — 45 Gated DeltaNet layers and 15 full softmax attention layers.
Neither DeepSeek-V3 nor GLM-5 use any linear attention.
Gated DeltaNet is a recurrent linear attention mechanism.
Instead of accumulating a growing KV cache (O(n) memory), it maintains a fixed-size recurrent state (O(1) memory) that summarizes all past context.
In each step, it:
1). Projects input → Q, K, V through a joint projection + causal 1D convolution (kernel=4) for local context mixing before the recurrence
2). L2-normalizes Q and K to stabilize the recurrent state updates
3). Computes decay: g = -exp(A_log) × softplus(alpha + dt_bias) — controls the forgetting rate of the recurrent state, where A_log is a learned base decay rate, alpha is input-dependent, and dt_bias is a per-head time-step bias
4). Computes write strength: beta = sigmoid(learned_projection) — controls how much of the error-correcting delta (difference between desired value and what the state currently retrieves) gets written into the recurrent state
5). Updates recurrent state: S_t = decay × S_{t-1} + beta × K_t × (V_t - S_{t-1}^T K_t)^T — combining forgetting of old state with error-correcting writes
6). Gates output through SiLU + RMSNorm with a separate z projection — gives the model per-token control over how much of the recurrent state's output flows to the next layer
The linear attention uses 16 key heads × 128 dims and 64 value heads × 128 dims — each key head is shared across 4 value heads, reducing key projection cost while maintaining a richer value representation.
Therefore, in Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, 75% of layers have zero KV cache. Only the 15 full-attention layers maintain one.
This is fundamentally different from DeepSeek-V3/GLM-5 which compress KV via MLA but still maintain it in every layer.
---
2. FULL ATTENTION LAYERS: GATED SOFTMAX WITH QK-NORM
The remaining 25% of layers use Grouped Query Attention (GQA), but modified in two important ways:
1). Gated output:
The q_proj outputs 2× normal size (hidden_size → num_heads × head_dim × 2) — half becomes the query, half becomes a sigmoid gate that modulates the attention output.
2). QK-Norm:
RMSNorm applied per-head to both Q and K before RoPE. Essential for stability with head_dim=256.
head_dim=256 is notably larger (Qwen 3: 128).
But only 25% of those 256 dims receive RoPE positional encoding (partial_rotary_factor=0.25).
So 64 dims carry position info, 192 are position-agnostic.
DeepSeek-V3/GLM-5 achieve a similar nope/rope split through Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)'s decomposed projections — Qwen does it with standard GQA + partial RoPE, which is simpler.
Worth noting that the GQA in Qwen 3.5, though standard, is more aggressive: 32 query heads, but only 2 KV heads (16× grouping).
This minimizes KV cache in the 15 full-attention layers — each stores only 2 heads × 256 dims = 512 dims of key and value per token.
Combined with the 75% of layers that have no KV cache at all, the total KV memory footprint is a fraction of what a standard 60-layer transformer would require.
---
3. MoE: BIGGEST EXPERT POOL AMONG FRONTIER MODELS
512 softmax-routed experts + 1 sigmoid-gated shared expert, 10 selected per token.
This is the most fine-grained expert decomposition at the frontier. For comparison:
- DeepSeek-V3: 256 experts, 8 per token
- GLM-5: 256 experts, 8 per token
- Qwen 3.5: 512 experts, 10 per token
Qwen doubles the expert count and increases active experts by 25%, while reducing the activation ratio.
More experts with lower activation = more specialized routing.
Routing uses softmax (not sigmoid like DeepSeek-V3/GLM-5), with standard auxiliary loss (coef=0.001) for load balancing.
No e_score_correction_bias, no grouped routing.
The shared expert is back — Qwen 3 MoE had removed it entirely.
Qwen 3.5 restores it from the Qwen 2 MoE design, with a learned sigmoid gate that modulates the shared expert's contribution per token.
DeepSeek-V3/GLM-5 add their shared expert unconditionally (no gate).
Every layer uses MoE FFN — no dense-then-MoE pattern like DeepSeek-V3/GLM-5's first-3-dense approach.
---
4. CONTEXT AND POSITION ENCODING
262k context window — the longest among frontier MoE models (DeepSeek-V3: ~164k, GLM-5: ~203k).
This is enabled by two factors:
- an exceptionally high rope_theta=10,000,000 (10M) for the full-attention layers (DeepSeek-V3: 10K, GLM-5: 1M)
- and the linear attention layers that inherently handle arbitrary-length sequences with fixed-size state.
For position encoding, Qwen 3.5 uses MRoPE (Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding) with 3D position IDs (temporal, height, width) and interleaved frequency layout [THWTHW...].
With head_dim=256 and partial_rotary_factor=0.25, the rotary dim is 64. RoPE operates on pairs of dimensions, so that's 32 frequency pairs total.
mrope_section=[11, 11, 10] splits those 32 pairs across the three spatial axes: 11 for temporal, 11 for height, 10 for width.
For text-only input, all three position dimensions increment identically — equivalent to standard 1D RoPE.
The 3D structure activates when vision tokens enter the sequence: image patches receive their actual (height, width) spatial coordinates, and video frames receive distinct temporal indices.
This is what enables the native multimodal integration discussed next — the position encoding itself is designed to be spatially aware from the ground up, rather than treating visual tokens as flat sequential positions.
---
5. NATIVE MULTIMODAL: NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT
This is the other major differentiator from DeepSeek-V3 and GLM-5 (both text-only).
Qwen 3.5 is natively multimodal — the same 397B-parameter model handles text, images, and video.
No separate VLM variant needed.
The vision encoder is a 27-layer ViT (hidden=1152, 16 heads, head_dim=72) that uses strikingly different design choices from the language model:
- LayerNorm instead of RMSNorm,
- GELU instead of SiLU,
- standard MHA with bias instead of bias-free GQA,
- and non-causal attention.
It's as if two different design philosophies coexist within one model.
Patch embedding is a 3D convolution: Conv3d with kernel [2, 16, 16] (temporal × height × width).
This means video is handled natively — 2 consecutive frames are consumed at once to produce one spatiotemporal token per 2×16×16 volume.
Academic VLMs typically sample video frames individually and treat them as separate images.
The vision encoder uses dual position encoding: learned absolute embeddings (nn.Embedding with 48×48 = 2304 entries, bilinearly interpolated for arbitrary resolutions) plus 2D rotary position embeddings within attention.
After the transformer blocks, a PatchMerger groups 2×2 adjacent patches, concatenates their features (1152×4 = 4608), and projects through a 2-layer MLP to the LLM dimension (4096).
This reduces vision tokens by 4× before injection.
Vision-language integration uses direct token replacement: image/video features are scattered into the text sequence via masked_scatter at placeholder token positions (image_token_id=248056, video_token_id=248057).
The LLM's MRoPE then computes 3D position IDs — text tokens get identical values across temporal/height/width (equivalent to 1D), while vision tokens get their actual 2D spatial positions (row, col).
This gives the transformer genuine spatial awareness of visual content.
This contrasts sharply with the academic VLM approach (LLaVA, InternVL, etc.):
- Academic VLMs use a frozen off-the-shelf vision encoder (CLIP/SigLIP) + frozen pre-trained text LLM, connected by a trained adapter
- The LLM itself is architecturally unchanged — standard 1D position encoding, no spatial awareness
- Vision tokens get flat sequential positions with no height/width information
- Video support requires frame sampling + treating each frame as an independent image
- Training is multi-stage: first align the projector, then instruction-tune
Qwen 3.5 modifies the LLM itself for multimodal understanding.
MRoPE gives the transformer spatial position awareness.
The vision encoder is custom-designed to match the LLM's expectations.
The model is trained end-to-end.
This is a fundamentally deeper integration than the adapter-based paradigm.
---
6. OTHER NOTABLE DETAILS
- RMSNorm uses (1 + weight) formulation with zero initialization (Gemma 2/3 style), not standard weight-initialized-to-ones
- Vocab expanded to 248,320 (from 151,936 in Qwen 3, +63%)
- MTP (Multi-Token Prediction): 1 additional prediction layer, weights ignored at inference (mtp.* prefix). Same training technique as DeepSeek-V3/GLM-5
- No attention bias anywhere in the LLM (Q/K/V/O projections, linear attention projections, conv1d — all bias-free). Vision encoder uses bias.
- Hybrid cache system: KV cache for full-attention layers, conv states + recurrent states for DeltaNet layers
---
7. THE CONVERGENCE, AND THE TWO CAMPS
The frontier MoE models have converged on the same skeleton: hundreds (256-512) of experts, ~8-10 active per token, shared expert, SwiGLU FFN, MTP training, no attention bias.
But the attention mechanism and multimodal strategy present the ongoing architectural debate.
Camp 1 — MLA + DSA, Text-Only (DeepSeek-V3, GLM-5):
- MLA compresses KV cache via low-rank latent projections
- DSA selects top-k tokens for sparse long-context attention
- Sigmoid routing with bias correction (no aux loss)
- Every layer is quadratic attention with compressed KV
- Text-only — VLM capability requires a separate model
Camp 2 — Linear Attention Hybrid, Native Multimodal (Qwen 3.5):
- GatedDeltaNet eliminates KV cache in 75% of layers
- Full GQA with gating in 25% of layers as "context checkpoints"
- Softmax routing with auxiliary loss
- 512 experts (2× the competition)
- Native vision-language with MRoPE, Conv3d video, and direct token integration
Both target the same core inference efficiency problem through fundamentally different mechanisms.
MLA compresses the cache; DeltaNet eliminates it.
DSA selects tokens; DeltaNet summarizes all past context in fixed-size state.
But Qwen 3.5 also stakes a position on multimodal architecture.
While DeepSeek-V3 and GLM-5 leave multimodal to derivative model families, Qwen makes the base model itself multimodal — with architectural modifications (MRoPE, 3D position IDs) that wouldn't be possible with the adapter-based approach used by most academic VLMs.
Bravo to the Qwen team — instead of adopting the DeepSeek's blueprint (as GLM-5 did), they bet on two genuinely different ideas:
1) that recurrent state machines beat compressed quadratic attention for efficient inference, and
2) that native multimodal integration beats the adapter paradigm.
Whether both bets pay off will be telling.
Quoting @zhuokaiz
The frontier exploration of LLM architectures has largely converged.
I dug through the HuggingFace transformers code for @Zai_org's newly released GLM-5 (zai-org/GLM-5).
Here's a detailed architectural breakdown, and what it tells us about where LLM design is heading.
TL;DR: Architecturally, GLM-5 closely follows DeepSeek-V3 with minor knob-tuning.
ATTENTION: MLA replaces GQA
The biggest change from GLM-4.7 to GLM-5 is attention.
GLM-4.7 used standard Grouped Query Attention (GQA) with 96 Q heads, 8 KV heads, separate q/k/v projections.
GLM-5 scraps all of that and adopts DeepSeek's Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA).
In the MLA pipeline, queries go through a LoRA-style two-stage projection:
hidden -> q_a_proj to rank 2048 -> RMSNorm -> q_b_proj to 64 heads * 256 dim.
Keys and values are jointly compressed into a single low-rank bottleneck:
hidden -> kv_a_proj to rank 512+64 -> split into a latent KV path and a RoPE path.
The latent part gets expanded back via kv_b_proj into 64 heads of (192 nope + 256 value) dims.
This is the exact same MLA design as DeepSeek-V3.
GLM-5 just tunes the dimensions: q_lora_rank 2048 vs 1536, v_head_dim 256 vs 128, qk_nope_head_dim 192 vs 128.
The kv_lora_rank (512) and qk_rope_head_dim (64) are identical.
Also, no bias anywhere in attention (attention_bias defaults to False).
Every projection (q_a_proj, q_b_proj, kv_a_proj, kv_b_proj, o_proj, and all DSA indexer projections) is bias-free.
This is now standard practice; among major models released in 2025, only GPT-oss still uses attention bias.
DSA: DeepSeek's Sparse Attention
GLM-5 adopts DeepSeek V3.2's native sparse attention (DSA) — this is the only architectural feature @Zai_org explicitly highlighted.
The attention class carries dedicated indexer components: wq_b, wk, k_norm, and weights_proj, used to select the top-2048 most relevant tokens (index_topk=2048) for each attention step instead of attending over the full context.
MoE ROUTING: Same Recipe and Same Numbers
256 routed experts + 1 shared expert.
Same as DeepSeek-V3 on both counts; up from GLM-4.7's 128 routed experts.
So far, only the Qwen-3 series has removed the shared expert — everyone else keeps one.
Top-8 experts selected per token (num_experts_per_tok=8).
Sigmoid-based routing (not softmax) with e_score_correction_bias for load balancing — no auxiliary loss at all, exactly like DeepSeek-V3.
Top-k weights are normalized (norm_topk_prob=True), then scaled by routed_scaling_factor = 2.5 — identical to DeepSeek-V3 (GLM-4.7 used 1.0).
moe_intermediate_size = 2048, also identical to DeepSeek-V3.
One simplification vs DeepSeek-V3: GLM-5 drops grouped expert selection entirely (n_group=1, topk_group=1).
DeepSeek-V3 divides 256 experts into 8 groups of 32 and selects top-4 groups before picking experts within them.
GLM-5 skips this and just does flat top-8 across all 256.
This is consistent with GLM-4.7's approach — suggesting grouped routing may not be essential.
FFN / MLP: SwiGLU, dense-then-MoE
All feed-forward (FFN) layers use SwiGLU (gated linear unit with SiLU activation), with no bias in any projection.
This applies to dense FFNs, routed experts, and shared experts alike.
The 78 layers follow a dense-then-MoE pattern: the first 3 layers use a standard dense FFN (intermediate_size=12288), and the remaining 75 layers are all MoE — no dense/MoE interleaving within the MoE region.
DeepSeek-V3 uses the same 3-dense-then-MoE split.
GLM-4.7 used only 1 initial dense layer.
Within each MoE layer, the output is the sum of two parts:
(1) the routed expert mixture (top-8 out of 256, each with intermediate_size=2048),
and (2) a shared expert (also intermediate_size=2048) that processes every token unconditionally.
MODEL SKELETON: 78 layers, 202k context
78 transformer layers total (deeper than DeepSeek-V3's 61). hidden_size = 6144.
64 attention heads, 64 KV heads (MLA makes the effective KV much cheaper than this number suggests).
RMSNorm throughout (eps=1e-5).
Vocab size 154,880.
Word embeddings are not tied to the LM head by default (tie_word_embeddings=False).
Context length is 202,752 tokens.
RoPE uses interleaved layout (rope_interleave=True), again importing apply_rotary_pos_emb_interleave directly from DeepSeek-V3.
The code supports YaRN scaling via yarn_get_mscale, but rope_theta and rope_type are set in the model's config.json rather than hardcoded in the source.
MTP: Multi-Token Prediction
Multi-Token Prediction is a training technique (popularized by DeepSeek-V3) where the model learns to predict multiple future tokens simultaneously through extra prediction heads, improving representation quality.
These extra heads are only used during training and discarded at inference time.
GLM-5 appears to use MTP, as the model checkpoint contains weights for a 79th decoder layer (model.layers.78), one beyond the 78 regular layers (indices 0-77).
The transformers code explicitly skips these extra weights when loading the model.
DeepSeek-V3 and GLM-4.7 both exhibit the same pattern — extra layer weights in the checkpoint, ignored at load time — consistent with how MTP training heads are typically shipped and discarded.
WHAT THIS MEANS
GLM-5 didn't just borrow a few ideas from DeepSeek.
It
- replaced its entire attention mechanism (GQA -> MLA)
- adopted DSA
- adopted sigmoid MoE routing with e_score_correction_bias
- doubled its expert count to match DeepSeek's 256,
- matched the routing scaling factor (2.5), expert intermediate size (2048), and number of initial dense layers (3)
- and adopted MTP.
The only thing GLM-5 clearly kept from its own GLM-4.7 lineage — where it differs from DeepSeek-V3 — is flat top-k routing without grouped selection (n_group=1 vs DeepSeek's 8).
However, this is NOT a bad thing.
When a major lab scraps its own architectural lineage and rebuilds on a competitor's blueprint — matching not just the design patterns but many of the key hyperparameters — it means the design space has been explored.
MLA + sigmoid MoE + shared experts + no aux loss + DSA + MTP is becoming the standard frontier MoE recipe.
The returns to architectural novelty are diminishing.
The differentiation (for now) lies more in data curation, training recipes, and inference infrastructure, and less in the transformer block itself (but maybe we will see more architectural changes, or even non-transformer block in the future).

summary:
Ok but like, that arxiv plot was going exponential before ChatGPT. Let’s not blame LLMs here. Are there fake papers? Possibly, but submissions have been going crazy since I started gradschool in 2018. It’s the most exciting and accessible field of science in human history. Of course there are a lot of papers.
Quoting @Andrew_Akbashev
A really dangerous situation. Too many submissions. Too many generated papers. Little responsibility.
1. In 2026, more than 24,000 submissions were made to the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML). It’s TWO times more than in 2025. To fight it, the organizers now require researchers to pay $100 for every subsequent paper.
2. LLM adoption has increased researcher productivity by 90% (there’s a recent paper in Science).
3. The number of papers is becoming far too high. Submissions to arXiv have risen by 50% since 2022.
4. There are simply not enough reviewers. Plus, many scientists no longer want to invest precious time in it for free.
5. We can’t easily identify AI-made papers from the genuine ones.
__
Important words from Paul Ginsparg, a co-founder of arXiv:
“AI slop frequently can’t be discriminated just by looking at abstract, or even by just skimming full text. This makes it an “existential threat” to the system.”
Basically, we’re getting closer to the tipping point.
📍 Many professors blame the AI.
But the problem is likely elsewhere:
1. Without a sufficient number of papers, many PIs can’t get funded. They have to prove their credibility to reviewers. Their proposals have to rely on prior publications. In many countries, there are some informal (or even formal) expectations for how many papers a group with a certain size has to publish to survive (funding-wise).
2. Our students / postdocs need papers if they want to be hired in faculty roles. Yes, some departments hire people with few publications. But the majority still want to ensure their faculty can get funded. If funding is partly a function of papers, this is used in decision-making.
3. The number of papers is important if you want to get high-level awards. Many of them are not given because you published one paper (even if it’s great). They are given because you made a meaningful CONTRIBUTION to the field. How do you make it? Publish more papers.
4. Tenure promotions in many places take the number of your papers into account (often indirectly). Your tenure may get delayed if you don’t publish enough. Not everywhere, but for many mid- to low-ranked universities this story is more or less the same.
+ There are many more to mention.
📍My opinion:
Much of this is rooted in how funding is distributed.
There is a strong correlation between the requirements at a university and the funding acquisition criteria.
If funding were based ONLY on the quality of published papers, universities would hire people for the quality of their science. If funding agencies strongly discouraged publishing too many papers, universities wouldn’t expect numbers from faculty during promotions. And some supervisors wouldn’t pressure students and postdocs to publish unfinished studies and low-quality data.
Yes, we need good detectors of fake papers.
But we also need the right policies and better funding allocation criteria.

All @SemiAnalysis_ posts are now legally required to add tone indicators /gen
Quoting @SemiAnalysis_
SERIOUS & PROFESSIONAL: The extreme register pressure did not let up on Hopper, which motivated Blackwell to include Tensor Memory (TMEM), a new piece of memory specialized for Tensor Core operations. On every SM, TMEM has 128 rows (lanes) and 512 columns of 4-byte cells, totaling to 256 KB, which is also the size of the register file on an SM.
TMEM has a restricted memory access pattern. Specifically, it takes a warpgroup to access the whole TMEM, and each warp in a warpgroup can only access a specific set of lanes. By limiting the memory access pattern, hardware designers can reduce the number of access ports, saving chip space. On the other hand, this design also means that epilogue operations need a warpgroup to operate. Unlike shared memory, programmers have to explicitly manage TMEM, including allocation, deallocation, and copying data in and out of TMEM. Our 2025 NVIDIA Tensor Core Evolution article talks more about this in depth
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCcBCTDWcAAZwSy.jpg

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
Ironically, this post is even more misleading. SWE-bench came out in 2023, which is ancient in this field. At the time, LMs were so shit at coding that people in the field believed the benchmark was literally impossible, basically the polar opposite of how the benchmark is viewed now.
SWE-Bench was a very good target for labs to gauge how well their models could do general coding tasks beyond just olympiad coding (which is basically just math). Sure, you could argue now that the original benchmark has saturated and is no longer a measure of progress for future models. But that's not the point, nor did the paper ever make the claim that getting high scores = you can replace SWEs in your company.
For the period where it wasn't saturated (2023-early 2025) it was genuinely a great marker of progress for LMs in coding. New evals have since come out and will continue to come out. It convinced the entire industry that "agents have the capability of eventually being good enough to do real work", which IMO was a huge deal.
Quoting @GarrettLord
Hot take: SWE-bench is the most misleading benchmark in AI. Not because it's bad - it's well built.
But because it convinced an entire industry that "agents can do real work" when really what they showed is agents can do one very specific type of work that happens to be easy to verify. This CMU paper shows agent success rates collapse as complexity increases.
Now imagine deploying that same agent on a $30M JPMorgan compliance workflow. You'd get fired in a week.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCgzQk7awAAIGrm.jpg

One of the many examples why LLM tooling matters a lot. There's several 10x+ gains to be had just by improving the LLM tool interfaces and LLM runner history management. We could achieve so much more with the LLMs we currently have if we tooled them better.
Quoting @om_patel5
claude code has a hidden setting that makes it 600x faster and almost nobody knows about it
by default it uses text grep to find functions.
it doesn't understand your code at all. that's why it takes 30-60 seconds and sometimes returns the wrong file
there's a flag called ENABLE_LSP_TOOL that connects it to language servers. same tech that powers vscode's ctrl+click to jump straight to the definition
after enabling it:
> "add a stripe webhook to my payments page" - claude finds your existing payment logic in 50ms instead of grepping through hundreds of files
> "fix the auth bug on my dashboard" - traces the actual call hierarchy instead of guessing which file handles auth
> after every edit it auto-catches type errors immediately instead of you finding them 10 prompts later
also saves tokens because claude stops wasting context searching for the wrong files
2 minute setup and it works for 11 languages
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HC20PVeXAAA2tAe.jpg

This has been an open secret at labs for a while now. Great to see more work explaining how to use it!
Quoting @fujikanaeda
Checkpoint merging and evaluation (a la WSM) has also been a really fun project that I've gotten to drive within Nemotron.
Checkpoint merging gives us a cheap way to estimate eventual model performance without early decays (training time savings!) as well as Pareto buffet of possible final model choices to choose from at the end of training.
We've been able to reproduce results from WSM at increasing scale, but more work remains on finding merge strategies for surpassing and replacing very long decay entirely (e.g. the 5T we do for Nemotron 3).
The checkpoint we selected from pretraining for mid & post-training was a 500B token window merge at 25B token intervals using minus-sqrt decay emulation :)

Introducing 𝑨𝒕𝒕𝒆𝒏𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏 𝑹𝒆𝒔𝒊𝒅𝒖𝒂𝒍𝒔: Rethinking depth-wise aggregation.
Residual connections have long relied on fixed, uniform accumulation. Inspired by the duality of time and depth, we introduce Attention Residuals, replacing standard depth-wise recurrence with learned, input-dependent attention over preceding layers.
🔹 Enables networks to selectively retrieve past representations, naturally mitigating dilution and hidden-state growth.
🔹 Introduces Block AttnRes, partitioning layers into compressed blocks to make cross-layer attention practical at scale.
🔹 Serves as an efficient drop-in replacement, demonstrating a 1.25x compute advantage with negligible (<2%) inference latency overhead.
🔹 Validated on the Kimi Linear architecture (48B total, 3B activated parameters), delivering consistent downstream performance gains.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
This article is pretty interesting and thought provoking but I feel like it doesn't really connect its two ideas core ideas.
Which is what we are observing in coding agents and then what our future looks like when its over.
It makes strong arguments about the "Double-Whammy" of increased capabilities
1. Increased capabilities = increased complexity
2. Increased capabilities = higher stakes deployments
Higher stakes = less room for mistakes.
Things are harder to test, and depolyments are higher stakes (that seems really bad and worth chewing on for a bit)
but then it just kind of accepts
"But someday, agents will have no problems left, and we’ll be left figuring out what to do with ourselves. And until that day, you’ll need production monitoring."
Maybe the author's take here can be interpreted as we will look back and think the problems agents have now are silly.
That may be true, but it still leaves us with a very likely painful transition period where people who move to quickly and carelessly have catastrophic infrastructural and legal complications on a scale we may have never witnessed before. And THIS is the good outcome where agents *DO* figure out everything eventually.
Quoting @benhylak

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
I’m not going to say frontier models with good harnesses can’t solve incredibly difficult problems.
I will say many people who tried fine tuning circa 2022-2024 were just way to earlier.
The base models at the time just weren’t good enough to meaningfully be improved. The methods for generating training data were terrible, using models as judges was not economic or reliable and paying for human annotations was too far out of reach.
Fast forward to 2026 and many people have developed sophisticated and realistic evaluation environments which if you squint look a lot like what you want for RL.
Cost of tokens is way down and the intelligence per token is much higher.
Training infrastructure is much simpler to setup, algorithms and data are better.
It’s more possible than it has ever been to adapt models to solve real world problems with a small team.
Quoting @mikiane
Mistral lance Forge pour fine-tuner.
95% des boîtes n'en ont pas besoin.
Un frontier + RAG + tools bat un fine-tuning custom. À chaque fois.
Fine-tuning = 2023
Orchestration = 2026

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
This is why @allen_ai is so important - it's an organization philosophically committed to complete open-source. It doesn't open-source to generate traction/investor money to then go closed source later (or farm community goodwill w/ OSS releases in order to then offer premium, closed-source models) - it open-sources as that's its ideological commitment. Even if its models aren't SOTA, the fact is that its current models are OSS and as long as it has the backing, it will keep making OSS models.
And this is important, as OSS today doesn't guarantee OSS tmrw. It's unclear if Minimax 2.7 will be OSS. If Qwen4 wlil be OSS. GLM-5 Turbo is a closed-source beta. Minimax 2.5, Qwen3.5, and GLM-5 may be open-source, but they are ultimately made by commercial companies with commercial goals who take their models closed-source when they wish.
So while I may use the above models now, I can rest assured that Olmo 4, and Olmo 5, and Olmo N, will all be open-source if they exist. There will not be a more-capable Olmo locked behind an API. We will always know how Olmo models are made, have the data they were trained on, and the intermediate checkpoints. And that's incredibly, incredibly valuable.
Quoting @natolambert
Qwen is irreplaceable. Has been going from strength to strength in recent times.
Things will always be different, I'm hopeful we can find groups of other models to fill the void.
RIP

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
I’m not going to say frontier models with good harnesses can’t solve incredibly difficult problems.
I will say many people who tried fine tuning circa 2022-2024 were just way to earlier.
The base models at the time just weren’t good enough to meaningfully be improved. The methods for generating training data were terrible, using models as judges was not economic or reliable and paying for human annotations was too far out of reach.
Fast forward to 2026 and many people have developed sophisticated and realistic evaluation environments which if you squint look a lot like what you want for RL.
Cost of tokens is way down and the intelligence per token is much higher.
Training infrastructure is much simpler to setup, algorithms and data are better.
It’s more possible than it has ever been to adapt models to solve real world problems with a small team.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
Finally found the official thread. Congrats on the release!
Quoting @bharatrunwal2
Introducing PRISM: Demystifying Retention and Interaction in Mid-Training
The modern LLM training pipeline has evolved beyond just pre-training + alignment. State-of-the-art models now insert a critical middle stage "mid-training" where targeted, high-quality data mixtures build reasoning foundations before RL. Yet despite its growing adoption, the field lacks a principled understanding of what actually drives its effectiveness.
— What data should you use?
— When in the pipeline should you mid-train?
— How does it interact with downstream RL?
— Does it generalize across architectures and scales?
— And beyond benchmarks: what do these stages actually do to the model at the weight and representation level?
These questions don't have clear answers in the literature at scale : and the cost of getting them wrong is significant.
PRISM is our systematic attempt to answer all of these. Using ~27B high-quality tokens, we run controlled experiments across 7 models · 4 families · 3B–24B parameters, spanning both dense Transformers and attention-Mamba hybrids, measuring what mid-training actually does: to performance, to weights, to representations, and to downstream RL.
🧵 Key findings below.

summary:
Many such cases 😎
Quoting @bharatrunwal2
The single biggest lever in mid-training design is Data Composition.
We ablated math-only, math+code, and math+code+science mixtures across models. The pattern is consistent:
Math only → large math gains, science stays near base
Math+Code → math and code gains, science still near base
Math+Code+Science → best overall, and the one that transforms GPQA-Diamond during RL
Including science at mid-training unlocks +17 to +28 points on GPQA-Diamond when you add RL later, even if the RL data mix never changes. The capability is seeded at mid-training, not at RL.
Changing the RL mix? Less than 2 point difference. The Data composition decisions belong at mid-training.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HD70OjqaoAA6RU2.jpg

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
This is very insightful.
Although it feels obvious after the fact, it makes sense that context length extension is a prerequisite for getting the most out of reasoning traces and SFT like data that tend to be much longer than documents seen in pretraining.
Although many tech reports include sections about what was done during long context extension we rarely get to see how the decision was made, or what was ablated.
As midtraining has become more common the secret art of how and why to blend what is happening with all the goals of preparing the model for post-training is finally getting the attention it deserves.
Quoting @bharatrunwal2
When should you mid-train?
We tested this on Granite-4 Micro: before vs. after long-context pretraining.
Mid-training after long-context pretraining gives the largest gains in math, code, and science while preserving general reasoning. Mid-training at 8k context degrades long-context ability, but this can be largely restored via a brief extension phase combined with model merging.
This also points to a broader principle: reasoning data for math, code, and especially long-CoT traces or agentic workflows tends to be long. A model needs sufficient context representation before it can fully absorb this data during mid-training. We did not test agentic traces in this work, but the same logic applies.
We only tested the timing question on Granite-4 Micro, so we are careful not to over-generalize. But practically: most open-source base models today are already released after long-context extension, so if you are starting from LLaMA-3.1, Mistral, Granite-3.3, or Nemotron-H, you are likely already at the right entry point.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HD8BVmYakAAfezm.png

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
summary:
These two statements resonate with me so much:
the real research "signals" come from the failures and surprises during the experimental process, not from armchair theorizing [02:08:12].
Publishing a paper is about sharing a profound realization with the world to find resonance and intellectual kinship, rather than just changing the world by force [01:31:27].
It’s so easy when getting started in research to get caught up in the publication race, and trying to build a brand, or get a job. The thing is doing good science pays long term dividends.
Sometimes it hurts, but you have to write the paper that your results are telling you, and as you mature sometimes you begin to find joy in your failures. When something truly doesn’t work that you expect that is often more informative then trying to fit results into your framework and narrative.
Quoting @kyleichan
6. The Influence of Kaiming He
Xie deeply admires Kaiming He, with whom he worked closely at FAIR. He learned that Kaiming's superpower is his extreme focus and ability to build an impenetrable baseline ("scaffold") before aiming for breakthroughs [02:34:30]. Kaiming taught him that the real research "signals" come from the failures and surprises during the experimental process, not from armchair theorizing [02:08:12].
7. "Impact" vs. "Understanding"
Xie dislikes the word "impact," finding it too ego-driven and aggressive. Instead, he views research through the lens of philosopher Hannah Arendt: the goal of research is "understanding." Publishing a paper is about sharing a profound realization with the world to find resonance and intellectual kinship, rather than just changing the world by force [01:31:27].
8. Intelligence is More Than Human Language
Xie cautions against human arrogance in defining intelligence solely through language. Drawing on evolutionary biology, he argues that building an AI with the survival and physical reasoning skills of a squirrel is actually a much harder problem than building an AI that can write code or pass exams [06:13:05].
9. The Power of "Research Taste"
Xie equates research to filmmaking, where "taste" dictates everything from the problem you choose to solve down to the formatting of the paper. Influenced by Kaiming He (who even gifted him the Buddhist Diamond Sutra to teach him to look past superficial "forms" to find true substance), Xie believes good taste means avoiding crowded, hyped areas in favor of fundamental, eternal problems like representation learning [02:45:03].
10. The Degradation of Open Academic AI Research
Xie expresses concern over how major industrial AI labs have become increasingly closed off, shifting from open academic exploration to secretive commercial competition. This shift strips researchers of their autonomy and turns them into easily replaceable cogs in a massive engineering machine, heavily motivating his decision to start a new, more open research-driven company [05:21:26].

Jevons paradox is happening in real time. Companies, especially outside of tech, are realizing that they can now afford to take on software projects that they wouldn’t have been able to tackle before because now AI lets them do so.
We’re going to start to use software for all new things in the economy because it’s incrementally cheaper to produce. Marketing teams at big companies will have engineers helping to automate workflows. Engineers in life sciences and healthcare will automate research. Small businesses will hire engineers for the first to build better digital experiences.
And as long as AI agents still require a human who understands what to prompt, how to review when an agent goes off the rails, how it guide back, how to maintain the system that was built, how to fix the ongoing bugs, and more, we will still have humans managing these agents.
This is why all the advice you get of not going into engineering is wrong. The world is going to increasingly be made up of software, and the people that understand it best will be in a strong economic position. This will happen in other roles as well where output goes up and demand increases.

Engineering job openings are at the highest levels we’ve seen in over 3 years
There are over 67,000 (!!!) eng openings at tech companies globally right now, with 26,000 just in the U.S. We don’t know if there would have been more open roles if not for AI or if AI is actually leading to more open roles, but since the start of this year, the increase in open eng roles is accelerating even more.

Today, we are emerging from stealth and launching PrismML, an AI lab with Caltech origins that is centered on building the most concentrated form of intelligence.
At PrismML, we believe that the next major leaps in AI will be driven by order-of-magnitude improvements in intelligence density, not just sheer parameter count.
Our first proof point is the 1-bit Bonsai 8B, a 1-bit weight model that fits into 1.15 GBs of memory and delivers over 10x the intelligence density of its full-precision counterparts. It is 14x smaller, 8x faster, and 5x more energy efficient on edge hardware while remaining competitive with other models in its parameter-class.
We are open-sourcing the model under Apache 2.0 license, along with Bonsai 4B and 1.7B models.
When advanced models become small, fast, and efficient enough to run locally, the design space for AI changes immediately. We believe in a future of on-device agents, real-time robotics, offline intelligence and entirely new products that were previously impossible.
We are excited to share our vision with you and keep working in the future to push the frontier of intelligence to the edge.

google gemma 4 architecture is very interesting and every model has some subtle differences, here is a recap:
> per layer embedding only on the small variant
> no attention scale (usually you divide qk^T by sqrt(d), they don't)
> they do QK norm + V norm as well
> they share K and V for the large variant
> they do quite aggressive KV cache sharing on the small variant
> sliding window (512 and 1024) is bigger than gpt-oss 128 and they don't use sinks!
> softcapping
> rope only on part of the dimensions + different rope theta for the local/global layer

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: The potential return of heavyweight software release processes
summary:
Honestly we probably needed better staging and testing for software anyways.
Quoting @danlovesproofs
Deep scans can unearth nasty vulnerabilities in basically any codebase. We're excited about a world beyond PR-level review because there's a limit to what you can find in a few minutes. The multi-hour domain lets you really exercise the code.
The results are so compelling we might see the return of a more heavyweight release process.
The code review bots are fantastic but nowhere near good enough to auto-merge everything they approve. Human code review is too time-consuming and is dubiously effective in the first place. And the models are getting so capable that shipping with vulns is an increasingly unacceptable risk.
So we may see a world shaped more like early 2010s software engineering than the continuous delivery we're all used to now: bona fide staging, fewer releases per day, and a QA phase with 10^15 GPU cycles before release.
SaaS unlocked deploy-on-merge, partially because fast deploy and direct prod access dramatically lowered the cost of a bug. If the internet becomes a dark forest of always-on 1000 IQ attackers, the cost of a bug is no longer low, your bar for deploy should be higher, and the eng practices we associate with outmoded non-tech-native companies might start to make sense for a 10 person SaaS.
clean_summary:
Honestly, we probably needed better staging and testing for software anyway. Deep scans can unearth nasty vulnerabilities in basically any codebase. There's a limit to what you can find in a few minutes, so multi-hour domain testing allows for a more thorough examination of the code.

The results are compelling enough that we might see a return to a more heavyweight release process. While code review bots are fantastic, they are not yet good enough to auto-merge everything they approve. Human code review is time-consuming and often ineffective. As models become more capable, shipping with vulnerabilities is an increasingly unacceptable risk. This shift may lead to practices reminiscent of early 2010s software engineering, with bona fide staging, fewer releases per day, and extensive QA phases before release.

clean_title: Partnership with Thomson Reuters to enhance legal models using proprietary data
summary:
Grateful to be working with @schwarzjn_ and his team at Thomson Reuters to help leverage their proprietary data to mid-train the world's best legal models!
Mid-training on domain specific data can massively improve specialized performance without sacrificing general capabilities. And because the mid-trained model understands the domain better, post-training becomes far more effective.
Check out our case study linked below to learn more. And if you want to leverage your own proprietary data to build strong, domain specific models where accuracy and reliability are key, please reach out to us @datologyai!
Quoting @datologyai
We’re excited to announce our partnership with Thomson Reuters, a collaboration focused on unlocking the full potential of proprietary data to build the next generation of domain-specific AI.
By applying DatologyAI’s data curation pipeline for legal domain adaptation mid-training, the results were clear:
- +5% improvement on legal benchmarks and +2.5% on general-purpose evaluations after mid-training
- >2.5x amplification in post-training gains on Thomson Reuters’ private legal evals
- Achieved with <1% of the original pre-training token budget
These gains demonstrate that better data doesn’t just improve models, but multiplies the effectiveness of everything built on top of them.
As @schwarzjn_ , Head of AI Research at Thomson Reuters, put it:
“DatologyAI delivered clear, measurable improvements across both public and our proprietary legal evaluations…demonstrating the strength and generalizability of their approach.”
This partnership shows what’s possible when proprietary data and advanced data curation come together — not just incremental gains, but compounding advantages across the entire model lifecycle.
We’re excited to continue building with Thomson Reuters to push the boundaries of domain AI.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: Insights on continual learning and memory storage
summary:
I actually really enjoyed this article on continual learning. Finally had a chance to read through over the weekend. Thanks to @a16z for the spotlight on our work at @adaption_ai
I think what the deep dive gets right is it correctly pinpoints one of the core questions researchers are thinking about in continual learning: what types of knowledge belong in different types of memory stores.
Our own memory is stored at different rates, with short term and long term memory stored in different parts of the brain. How we achieve this type of dual storage in our current algorithms is going to be one of the most fun questions of next 2 years.
The balance between parametric and non-parametric techniques and rapid innovation on the architectures, optimization and data for both will be important.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HG6hrV_aAAEuBK3.jpg

A company you’ve probably never heard of raised $475M six months ago to create a radically new way of building AI. No Von Neumann bottleneck, no memory bandwidth issues, hugely less power required.

NVIDIA, TPUs and similar chips will rule for the next five years at least, but at some point, a new way of building AI will emerge.
I don’t know if it’ll be found by @unconvAI or not, but I’m glad well funded companies like this are tackling this problem.

NVIDIA, TPUs, and similar chips will likely dominate for at least the next five years, but eventually, a new approach to building AI will emerge. While it's uncertain if @unconvAI will find this new method, it's encouraging to see well-funded companies tackling this challenge.

clean_title: Building in the open to achieve 1000x energy efficiency in AI
summary:
As I've said many times, we're building in the open @unconvAI . The first thing is to solve the problem, then fight about the market. @petermc 's blog below gives a skeleton of how we think about the problem of power efficiency. We have to go up and down the stack...it's not one magic bullet. It's the interaction of the model and the physics of the hardware. We need to do it all to realize 1000x. It's hard. But summiting K2 is only worth doing because it's hard :)
Quoting @unconvAI
Getting to 1000x energy efficiency in AI isn’t about one breakthrough.
It’s about solving two hard constraints:
1. Data movement dominates energy
2. Amdahl’s Law caps system-level gains
Which means you have to rethink everything: models, hardware, and how they’re designed together.
If this kind of problem excites you, you’ll enjoy our latest blog:

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: Reflections on memory-centric architecture in electronics and AI
summary:
Reminds me of a blog post I made... 21 years ago:
"It seems that the developmental trajectory of electronics is recapitulating the evolutionary history of the brain. Specifically, both are saturating with a memory-centric architecture. Is this a fundamental attractor in computation and cognition? Might a conceptual focus on speedy computation be blinding us to a memory-centric approach to artificial intelligence?
The mention of Moore’s Law conjures up images of speedy microprocessors. Logic chips used to be mostly made of logic gates, but today’s microprocessors, network processors, FPGAs, DSPs and other “systems on a chip” are mostly memory. And they are still built in fabs that were optimized for logic, not memory.
The IC market can be broadly segmented into memory and logic chips. The ITRS estimates that in the next six years, 90% of all logic chip area will actually be memory. Coupled with the standalone memory business, we are entering an era for complex chips where almost all transistors manufactured are for memory, not logic.
At the presciently named HotChips conference, AMD, Intel, Sony and Sun showed their latest PC, server, and PlayStation processors. They are mostly memory. In moving from the Itanium to the Montecito processor, Intel saturated the design with memory, moving from three megabytes to 26.5MB of cache memory. From a quick calculation (assuming 6 transistors per SRAM bit and error correction code overhead), the Montecito processor has ~1.5 billion transistors of memory, and 0.2 billion of logic. And Intel thought it had exited the memory business in the 80’s. |-)
Why the trend? The primary design enhancement from the prior generation is “relieving the memory bottleneck.” Intel explains the problem with their current processor: "For enterprise work loads, Itanium executes 15% of the time and stalls 85% of the time waiting for main memory.” When the processor lacks the needed data in the on-chip cache, it has to take a long time penalty to access the off-chip DRAM. Power and cost are also improved to the extent that more can be integrated on chip.
Weaving these brain and semi industry threads together, the potential for intelligence in artificial systems is ripe for a Renaissance. Hawkins ends his book On Intelligence with a call to action: “now is the time to start building cortex-like memory systems... The human brain is not even close to the limit” of possibility.
Hawkins estimates that the memory size of the human brain is 8 terabytes, which is no longer beyond the reach of commercial technology. The issue though, is not the amount of memory, but the need for massive and dynamic interconnect. I would be interested to hear from anyone with solutions to the interconnect scaling problem."
— from
.... just a trip down memory lane....
clean_summary:
Reminds me of a blog post I made 21 years ago discussing how the developmental trajectory of electronics mirrors the evolutionary history of the brain, particularly with a focus on memory-centric architecture. This raises questions about whether a focus on speedy computation might be overshadowing the potential of memory-centric approaches in artificial intelligence.

The blog post highlights that while Moore's Law emphasizes rapid microprocessor development, the reality is that modern microprocessors are increasingly memory-centric. The Integrated Circuit market is shifting, with projections indicating that 90% of logic chip area will be memory in the coming years. Major companies have demonstrated processors that prioritize memory, addressing the memory bottleneck that hampers performance.

As we weave together insights from brain function and semiconductor industry trends, there is potential for a renaissance in artificial intelligence. The call to action is to develop cortex-like memory systems, as the human brain's memory capacity is now within reach of commercial technology, although challenges remain in achieving effective interconnectivity.

clean_title: Hybrid format for efficient LLM sparsity and speed improvements
summary:
Time is a flat circle and all sparsity and distillation research is relevant again it seems.
Quoting @hardmaru
The human brain🧠 is incredibly efficient because it only activates the specific neurons needed for a thought. Modern LLMs naturally try to do this too (> 95% of neurons in feedforward layers stay silent for any given word), but our hardware punishes them for it.
One of the most frustrating paradoxes in deep learning: making a model do less math often makes it run slower. Why? Because unstructured sparsity introduces irregular memory access, and GPUs are built for predictable, dense blocks of math.
We teamed up with @NVIDIA to try to fix this hardware mismatch. Instead of forcing the GPU to adapt to the sparsity, we built a "Hybrid" format that reshapes the sparsity to fit the GPU. Our sparsity format (TwELL) dynamically routes the 99% of highly sparse tokens through a fast path, and uses a dense backup matrix as a safety valve for the rare, heavy tokens.
Through TwELL and a new set of custom CUDA kernels for both LLM inference and training, we translated theoretical sparsity into actual wall-clock speedups: >20% faster training and inference on H100 GPUs, while also cutting energy consumption and memory requirements.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: Need for transparency in model benchmark costs and compute usage
summary:
This has made me think that more model tech reports need to report the cost to run benchmarks, or maybe the compute used to achieve a given score. A lot can be hidden in just reporting throughput, latency, and benchmarks.
Test time compute *is* a great way to get better results, but if you need way more generation to match a larger model it isn't as obvious of a win. You can also run into context rot problems if every step requires significantly more generation.
Quoting @code_star
I tried reimplementing the DeepSeek hparam calculator web app I made in my substack article by giving gpt5.5 a screenshot and a description of what it should do.
Then, I had GPT 5.5, DeepSeekV4 Pro, and Kimi 2.6 attempt to implement it. Despite having very different token prices, they all completed at incredibly close final costs (about $1.20 – $1.50).
Ironically, DeepseekV4 Pro couldn't get it to work in a single shot.

summary:

I was proud of the work I did but felt as I finished my dissertation that it was actually going to be useless in the age of LLMs and scaling.
Everything I did at the time told me if you could just put more compute into training smaller models and they hadn’t saturated you should just keep doing that. In 2023 the idea of training any model over 1B parameters and seeing it fully “converge” was comical to me. Maybe we are getting there though.
What was old is new again. Train compute is plentiful and the economics of inference, the bottlenecks of memory and MoEs may force us to take a hard look at these methods that seemed to impractical a few years ago.

clean_title: The future of model development and collaboration
summary:
Making good models is really hard, but I think the future is bright ✨
Quoting @code_star
I think the problem is money is a necessary, but not sufficient condition for training good models. It’s a really hard structurally and organizational problem. You have to get everyone on the same page and trying to make “good models” and not simply hitting KPIs or advancing their own careers.
A lot of NeoLabs are specifically *not* going all in on trying to make generalist models.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: Reflections on a decade in academia
summary:
Ten years in academia and the best part has not been what many value most ie freedom to pursue your ideas. It’s experiencing your students grow and go on to incredible trajectories.
What I’ve come to know about myself is that I value permanence, presence, and people. And for all the illusions that institutions, titles, awards etc offer, none at all come close to this: watching a human absorb, even in tiny amounts, the care and effort you’ve put into trying your best to just be there for them.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: The hidden history of Ozempic and its early development
summary:
In some very real sense, Ozempic was invented in 1990. Pfizer ran the human trials and just never published them.
They showed it lowered blood glucose in diabetics, slowed gastric emptying, and killed hunger; the same 3 things that make Ozempic work today.
The joint venture agreement said internal data stayed internal, and that was that. Pfizer killed the program in 1991. The reasoning, as far as I can tell, was that nobody would ever want an injectable diabetes drug besides insulin.
So, the license went back to the hospital in Boston that held the patents.
Novo picked it up in 1992 and spent the next two decades building liraglutide, then semaglutide.
It's insane that data sat in a filing cabinet for 30+ years.
I only know this because Jeffrey Flier, one of the Harvard scientists in the room, finally wrote it up. He's in his late 70s and didn't want the history to die with him.
This makes you wonder what else is in those filing cabinets.
Ozempic could've existed 27 years ago.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIo9d52asAAhyK9.jpg
clean_summary: In a very real sense, Ozempic was invented in 1990 when Pfizer conducted human trials showing it lowered blood glucose, slowed gastric emptying, and suppressed hunger—effects that define Ozempic today. However, Pfizer never published these results and, under a joint venture agreement, kept the internal data secret before killing the program in 1991, believing no one would want an injectable diabetes drug besides insulin. The rights then reverted to a Boston hospital, and Novo acquired them in 1992, developing liraglutide and semaglutide over the following decades. It is astonishing that this data remained hidden in filing cabinets for over 30 years, a fact only revealed when Harvard scientist Jeffrey Flier documented it late in his life. This raises the question of what other medical history might still be stored away unseen.

clean_summary:
4 shared experts with 8 routed experts active? So 12 out of 132, that's quite high, and I wonder why. Most papers like Towards Greater Leverage suggest using 1 shared expert or minimal sharing; I think eventually we should decouple shared expert size.

Also, 128 attention heads with GQA? The configuration shows 218B parameters and 8 active experts—7 routed plus 1 shared, though the HF config mentions 4 shared. The model has a maximum context of 128K, which is relatively short. It uses SWA and full precision with a 2:1 ratio, and expert weights are W4A4 with NVFP4. The token router applies sigmoid then normalizes.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: AI development themes: from frontier labs to accessible research
summary:
My favorite reoccurring theme in AI model development is that each thing seemed to be too hard or outside of the reach of anyone but the frontier labs quickly collapses into one of the most accessible areas of research for people with relatively little compute.
A great example of this was reasoning models, verifiable rewards, and GRPO.
The researchers at OAI and Anthropic were insufferable to talk to at NeurIPS after O1 came out and the feeling was it was over for everyone not at those places. Then R1 came out and a few months later half of the grad students in america were doing GRPO on small math problems and doing interesting and meaningful research.
Quoting @zhengyaojiang
I actually thought pretraining would be the hardest part of recursive self-improvement, given how expensive it is to get ground-truth signals.
It’s interesting that Anthropic decided to start there.
A few hypotheses:
- With scaling laws, you can predict the final model after pretraining relatively reliably. This may not be the case for RLHF/RLVR.
- Lower-level work, like kernel engineering, is easier to measure with clear signals like speed, but reward hacking happens much more often.
- A lot of pretraining progress may mostly come from incremental changes, like hyperparameter tuning and stacking smaller architecture or optimizer tricks, while other parts of the stack may still require larger mechanism design.
clean_summary:
A recurring theme in AI model development is that tasks once considered too hard or only achievable by frontier labs quickly become accessible to researchers with relatively little compute. An example is reasoning models, verifiable rewards, and GRPO, which after initial skepticism, saw widespread adoption among grad students working on small math problems.

@zhengyaojiang notes that pretraining was thought to be the hardest part of recursive self-improvement due to the expense of ground-truth signals, but some hypotheses suggest that scaling laws can reliably predict final model performance after pretraining, whereas RLHF and RLVR may not follow the same predictability. Additionally, lower-level work like kernel engineering is easier to measure with clear signals, but reward hacking occurs more frequently. Much of the progress in pretraining may come from incremental improvements such as hyperparameter tuning and architecture tricks, while larger mechanism design challenges remain.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: Introspective X Training: Feedback Conditioning Improves Scaling Across all LLM Training Stages
summary:
It’s just training
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI8cG0EagAAaHQp.jpg
Quoting @rajammanabrolu
Ever wished we had fewer X-training hyphenates? Pre, mid, post etc. Why not just Training?
Trying to bridge the divides (and get all our friends into one team again), we intro *Introspective X Training*, an offline RL inspired method that scales effectively across any LLM stage by annotating your data with a thinking reward generated language critique!
Up to 2.8x FLOP efficiency + 5-10 point score gains (esp with math and code) at any stage from scratch to 24T tokens on 8b (active) sized models!! We burned much compute ablating so you wouldn't have to
Moral of the story is‼️don't throw out any data via filtering, just feedback condition it‼️
You can spend FLOPs up front on inference to *classify* data quality and then train so that tokens aren't all treated equally based on the feedback starting early in training itself. Right now they're really only separated out much later during mid/post training
This improves overall compute efficiency and gives us benchmark perf not possible with just baseline methods!
Paper here:
Thanks to @BrandoCui and @GXiming for leading this w/ @__SyedaAkter @davidjesusacu @hyunw_kim @jaehunjung_com Yuxiao Qu @shrimai_ @YejinChoinka
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/2057893761024442368/pu/img/XMuyqkXqE2XUJZEq.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/2057893761024442368/pu/vid/avc1/480x270/OWg3ClGr_6yE6who.mp4?tag=25
clean_summary:
It’s just training. The method, called Introspective X Training, is inspired by offline reinforcement learning and aims to unify different training phases by annotating data with language critiques that serve as a thinking reward.

This approach allows for more efficient use of FLOPs, achieving up to 2.8 times the efficiency and 5-10 point score improvements, especially in math and code tasks, across models from scratch to 24T tokens on 8B-sized models. Instead of filtering out data, it conditions feedback early in training, improving overall compute efficiency and benchmark performance beyond baseline methods.

summary:
It’s just training
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI8cG0EagAAaHQp.jpg
Quoting @rajammanabrolu
Ever wished we had fewer X-training hyphenates? Pre, mid, post etc. Why not just Training?
Trying to bridge the divides (and get all our friends into one team again), we intro *Introspective X Training*, an offline RL inspired method that scales effectively across any LLM stage by annotating your data with a thinking reward generated language critique!
Up to 2.8x FLOP efficiency + 5-10 point score gains (esp with math and code) at any stage from scratch to 24T tokens on 8b (active) sized models!! We burned much compute ablating so you wouldn't have to
Moral of the story is‼️don't throw out any data via filtering, just feedback condition it‼️
You can spend FLOPs up front on inference to *classify* data quality and then train so that tokens aren't all treated equally based on the feedback starting early in training itself. Right now they're really only separated out much later during mid/post training
This improves overall compute efficiency and gives us benchmark perf not possible with just baseline methods!
Paper here:
Thanks to @BrandoCui and @GXiming for leading this w/ @__SyedaAkter @davidjesusacu @hyunw_kim @jaehunjung_com Yuxiao Qu @shrimai_ @YejinChoinka
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/2057893761024442368/pu/img/XMuyqkXqE2XUJZEq.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/2057893761024442368/pu/vid/avc1/480x270/OWg3ClGr_6yE6who.mp4?tag=25
clean_summary:
It’s just training. The method, called Introspective X Training, is inspired by offline reinforcement learning and aims to improve large language model training by annotating data with language critiques that serve as a thinking reward.

This approach allows for up to 2.8 times more FLOP efficiency and 5-10 point score gains, especially in math and code tasks, across models from scratch to 24T tokens on 8B-sized models. Instead of filtering out data, it conditions feedback early in training, classifying data quality with inference FLOPs and adjusting training accordingly. This results in better compute efficiency and benchmark performance that baseline methods cannot achieve.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: Introspective X Training: Feedback Conditioning Improves Scaling Across all LLM Training Stages
summary:
Just refound one of my motivating memes for this paper from @kylelostat @soldni and co's COLM poster last year.
Made me wonder if we could fix that? It was getting out of hand now there were like 6 trainings.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJRfjZsaEAAAc6C.jpg
Quoting @rajammanabrolu
Ever wished we had fewer X-training hyphenates? Pre, mid, post etc. Why not just Training?
Trying to bridge the divides (and get all our friends into one team again), we intro *Introspective X Training*, an offline RL inspired method that scales effectively across any LLM stage by annotating your data with a thinking reward generated language critique!
Up to 2.8x FLOP efficiency + 5-10 point score gains (esp with math and code) at any stage from scratch to 24T tokens on 8b (active) sized models!! We burned much compute ablating so you wouldn't have to
Moral of the story is‼️don't throw out any data via filtering, just feedback condition it‼️
You can spend FLOPs up front on inference to *classify* data quality and then train so that tokens aren't all treated equally based on the feedback starting early in training itself. Right now they're really only separated out much later during mid/post training
This improves overall compute efficiency and gives us benchmark perf not possible with just baseline methods!
Paper here:
Thanks to @BrandoCui and @GXiming for leading this w/ @__SyedaAkter @davidjesusacu @hyunw_kim @jaehunjung_com Yuxiao Qu @shrimai_ @YejinChoinka
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/2057893761024442368/pu/img/XMuyqkXqE2XUJZEq.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/2057893761024442368/pu/vid/avc1/480x270/OWg3ClGr_6yE6who.mp4?tag=25
clean_summary:
Just refound one of my motivating memes for this paper from @kylelostat, @soldni, and colleagues' COLM poster last year. It made me wonder if we could fix that, as it was getting out of hand with like six trainings.

The tweet discusses *Introspective X Training*, an offline reinforcement learning inspired method that scales effectively across any large language model stage by annotating data with a language critique that acts as a thinking reward. This approach improves FLOP efficiency by up to 2.8 times and yields 5-10 point score gains, especially in math and code tasks, at any stage from scratch to 24T tokens on 8B-sized models. The method involves classifying data quality with inference FLOPs early in training, rather than filtering data later, which enhances overall compute efficiency and benchmark performance beyond baseline methods.

The linked paper provides detailed insights into how feedback conditioning can improve scaling in large language model training.

title: Cody Blakeney (@code_star)
clean_title: PithTrain: a compact, agent-native MoE training system
summary:
I feel like this is an interesting window into what future OSS software may look like.
Maximum hackable, confined within the limits of a set context length.
Quoting @ruihanglai
Two moments every ML researcher knows. You get onto a new cluster, and week one goes to fitting the framework to your setup, not training. A new architecture lands, and trying it means hacking through a gigantic codebase to stay compatible with the pipeline. What you want to change is small. The code you wade through to change isn't.
This experience is likely not alone, and many researchers we’ve talked to run into similar issues. A year of this on CMU's FLAME cluster left us with one question: what if a framework were built for an agent to adapt and evolve, not just for humans to maintain?
So we introduce PithTrain: a compact, agent-native MoE training system, now ~11K lines of Python, on four principles:
- Compact: fits in one context window
- Python-native: readable tracebacks, no compiled-extension rebuilds
- No implicit indirection: direct calls, each model in its own file
- Agent skills: in-repo playbooks for recurring tasks
Then we measured the thing nobody measures. Same agent, same tasks, only the framework underneath changes: on PithTrain it finishes with up to 62% fewer turns and 64% less GPU time than production frameworks, while training just as fast.
We call this second axis agent-task efficiency, and we believe it deserves to sit alongside training throughput as a metric worth optimizing. Excited to see what people build with it.
Built with amazing collaborators @haok1402, Haozhan Tang, Akaash Parthasarathy, @Zichun_Yu, @junrushao, Todd Mowry, @XiongChenyan and @tqchenml.
Blog:
Code:
Paper:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJvw00lWIAAlKvf.jpg
clean_summary:
This tweet discusses a new framework called PithTrain, which is designed to make machine learning research and training more efficient and adaptable. It is a small, Python-native system that fits within a single context window, with direct calls and in-repo playbooks for recurring tasks. PithTrain reduces training turns by up to 62% and GPU time by 64% while maintaining training speed, aiming to improve agent-task efficiency.

The idea is to create a framework that allows agents to adapt and evolve rather than just be maintained by humans, addressing common issues researchers face when trying to modify large, complex codebases. The work is supported by collaborations with multiple researchers and is documented through a blog, code repository, and arXiv paper.
